# Electrical panel and circuit notes

What the electrician explained while he was fixing the kitchen circuit.

## Why a breaker trips

A breaker trips to protect the wire. The common cause is an overload: too many appliances on one circuit, such as a microwave and a toaster plugged into the same kitchen circuit. Unplug something and move the appliances to outlets on different circuits. Never swap in a bigger breaker: the breaker is sized to the wire, and a larger one lets the wire overheat inside the wall before anything trips. A breaker that trips again and again, or trips with nothing running, means a short or a fault: leave it off and call an electrician.

## GFCI and AFCI protection

A GFCI outlet cuts power in a fraction of a second when current leaks to ground, and is required in kitchens, baths, garages and outdoors. Press its test button monthly. An AFCI breaker detects dangerous arcing in damaged wire and is required in bedrooms and living areas.

## Circuit sizes and big appliances

A 15-amp circuit with 14-gauge wire serves lights and ordinary outlets. Kitchen counters and bathrooms use 20-amp circuits with 12-gauge wire. An electric dryer needs its own 30-amp, 240-volt circuit with 10-gauge wire; an electric range needs 40 or 50 amps; an electric water heater needs 30 amps. A circuit that serves a big appliance must not share its outlet with anything else.

## Working in the panel

Only a licensed electrician should open the panel cover. The main breaker does not shut off the wires coming into the panel from the street, which stay live.

## Panel capacity and upgrades

Many older houses have 100-amp service; newer ones have 200 amps. Adding an electric car charger or a heat pump may need a load calculation and a panel upgrade. Changing the panel requires a permit and an inspection.
